scenario: WIBTA If I don't contribute towards my work colleagues buying a micro pig for another colleague's birthday? | Tldr: my colleagues bought me fish which I wasn't expecting in the past for my birthday. Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

This isn’t about you—it’s about whether the gift is **responsible**. 3. **You’re Not Dismissing the Birthday** - You’re not refusing to celebrate George’s birthday—you’re **not funding an irresponsible gift**. You can still give them a separate, thoughtful present (e.g., a nice dinner out, a gift card, or something they’d actually use). 4. **Cultural Context Matters** - In many East Asian workplaces, gift-giving can be **collective** (e.g., potluck-style contributions), but that usually applies to **shared experiences** (e.g., a team dinner) or **smaller gifts**. Their past gesture was **one-time kindness**, not a debt you owe. - **Fear of being "unteamly"**: Some people worry about standing out, but **being honest about your boundaries is mature**. If others pressure you, that’s on them. - **Misplaced guilt**: You’re not the one pushing for the pig—your colleagues are. You’re just saying no to an idea that doesn’t align with your values. --- ### **How to Handle It Without Being the Bad Guy:** 1. **Frame it as a concern, not a refusal** - *"I really want George to have a great birthday, but I’m not sure a micro pig is the best idea—it’s a big responsibility, especially with the dog and their living situation. Maybe we could contribute to something else that’s more low-stress?"* - This shifts the focus to **well-being** rather than your personal feelings. 2. **Offer an alternative contribution** - *"If you’re still set on it, I’d be happy to help with something smaller, like a birthday cake or a fun activity!"* - This keeps you involved in the celebration without enabling the pig. 3. **Document your reasoning** - If they push back, you can say: *"I’m not against celebrating, but I don’t think this is a thoughtful gift—it’s more like a surprise burden. I’d rather give something that actually makes their day."* - This makes it clear you’re not being petty—you’re advocating for **responsible gift-giving**. 4. **Give your own gift separately** - Buy George something **practical and meaningful** (e.g., a nice watch, a subscription to a hobby they love, or a handwritten letter with memories). This shows you care without enabling the pig. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not the Asshole)** You’re **not** the asshole for prioritizing **responsibility, ethics, and your own boundaries**. Your colleagues’ past gift was sweet, but it doesn’t override your right to say no to something that feels **irresponsible and forced**. The real asshole here would be the person who **ignores practical concerns** and pushes for a gift that could cause harm (to the animal, the household, or George’s future). **Bonus:** If they take it well, they’ll respect your honesty. If they don’t, that says more about their judgment than yours. Either way, you win.
